Uncover
ŭn-kŭv'ĕr
v. (to remove a covering; in the Law the standing euphemism for sexual sin, and the forbidden act of priestly mourning)
From un- (reversing) plus cover, Old French covrir, from Latin cooperire. In Scripture the word is the exact opposite of what God did for Adam and Eve, who were covered with coats of skins at the cost of a life.

Biblical Definition

Uncover is a covenant word with three distinct uses. In Leviticus 18 and 20 it is the fixed legal euphemism for sexual sin, and the chapter opens with the general prohibition: “None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD” (Lev 18:6). What follows is the incest code, and the closing verses ground it in creation and in judgment on the nations that practised otherwise. Second, it is forbidden to the priest in mourning: after the death of Nadab and Abihu, Moses says to Aaron and his surviving sons, “Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die” (Lev 10:6) — the ordinary signs of grief are denied to the man in office, because the priest represents God before the people even in his own bereavement. Third, it is a judicial act: in the trial of jealousy the priest is to “uncover the woman's head” (Num 5:18), an exposure before God in a case no human witness could settle.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines uncover as to divest of a cover; to remove a covering from; to lay open or expose to view; and also to deprive of clothes, to strip.

expand to see more

UNCOVER, v.t. To divest of a cover; to remove any covering from.

2. To deprive of clothes; to strip; to make naked.

3. To take the hat or cap from the head; to bare the head.

4. To lay open; to disclose; to reveal.

Note. To uncover the nakedness, in the Levitical law, is a phrase denoting unlawful commerce of the sexes.

Key Scripture

Lev 18:6 — "None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD."

Lev 10:6 — "And Moses said unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar and unto Ithamar, his sons, Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die, and lest wrath come upon all the people: but let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the LORD hath kindled."

Num 5:18 — "And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD, and uncover the woman's head, and put the offering of memorial in her hands, which is the jealousy offering: and the priest shall have in his hand the bitter water that causeth the curse:"

Isa 7:15 — "Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good."

Modern Corruption

Leviticus 18 is set aside as ritual purity law with no moral force, chiefly in order to detach its sexual prohibitions from any claim on the present.

expand to see more

The standard move in affirming readings of Scripture is to sort the Levitical material into ceremonial rules that lapsed with the temple and moral rules that abide, and then to place chapter 18 in the first pile. The chapter itself blocks this. Its prohibitions are grounded not in Israel's cultic distinctiveness but in what the Canaanites did and why the land vomited them out (Lev 18:24-28) — and the nations were not under the ceremonial law. The New Testament reasons the same way: Paul rebukes the Corinthian church for a case of a man with his father's wife, calls it fornication not named among the Gentiles, and applies the Levitical categories directly (1Co 5:1).

Lev 10:6 addresses a different reader, and a harder one. Aaron has just lost two sons under judgment, and he is forbidden the ordinary signs of grief because he is in office and the office is not his own. The passage does not deny grief — the whole house of Israel is to bewail the burning — but it does say that a man who stands between God and the people bears a restraint that others do not. Every elder and pastor who has had to carry a private sorrow through a public duty has stood in Aaron's place, and the text is a comfort as well as a demand: he stayed at the altar, and God kept him there.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English un- + cover; rendering Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover, remove, and hence to go into exile — one root for nakedness, revelation, and captivity.

expand to see more

Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, reveal, and to be carried away captive; exile is the nation stripped and exposed.

Hebrew galah ervah — “to uncover nakedness”; the standing legal formula for unlawful sexual union in Lev 18 and 20.

Hebrew ervah (H6172) — nakedness, shame, indecency; the noun behind the euphemism.

Hebrew para (H6544) — to let loose, uncover the head; Lev 10:6 and Num 5:18, the loosed hair of mourning and of accusation.

Gen 3:21 — the LORD God made coats of skins and clothed them; the covering God supplies at the cost of a life is the answer to every uncovering.

Usage

"“To uncover their nakedness” — the Law's fixed euphemism for sexual sin."

"“Uncover not your heads” — grief restrained in the man who holds the office."

"“Uncover the woman's head” — exposure before God where no witness could settle it."
